title: The Science of Sleep
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: For most of human history, sleep was regarded as a simple pause in life, a period of rest during which the body and brain did nothing of importance. Over the past fifty years that belief has been overturned. Brain scans show that the sleeping brain is highly active, and that different stages of sleep seem to carry out different tasks. Scientists now consider sleep to be as essential to health as food and water. Yet surveys in many countries suggest that busy adults treat it as the first thing to give up when life becomes crowded, and the consequences of that habit are only now being understood.

A night of sleep is not a uniform block. It is made up of cycles lasting about ninety minutes, each containing a period of light sleep, a period of deep sleep and a period of rapid eye movement, or REM, sleep, during which most vivid dreaming occurs. Early in the night deep sleep dominates; towards morning, REM periods grow longer. This pattern explains why people who wake after only five or six hours miss out on a disproportionate amount of REM sleep.

The link between sleep and memory has produced some of the most striking research. Dr Anna Voss asked two groups of students to learn a list of word pairs in the evening. One group slept normally; the other stayed awake all night. After two further nights of recovery sleep, both groups were tested, and the students who had slept on the first night remembered about a third more of the pairs. Voss concludes that sleep soon after learning helps to fix new information in the memory, and that a later night of rest cannot fully repair the loss.

Teenagers have attracted particular attention. During adolescence the body clock shifts, so that many young people do not feel sleepy until after eleven at night and find it hard to wake before eight in the morning. Professor Kenji Mori studied schools in three districts that moved the start of lessons from eight o'clock to half past nine. Attendance rose, and students reported feeling more alert, although their examination results improved only slightly. Mori admits that the improvement in grades might have been larger if students had not simply gone to bed later.

Napping is more controversial. Dr Leila Haddad found that a short nap of twenty minutes improved the performance of office workers on afternoon tasks, whereas naps longer than forty minutes left many of them feeling groggy. She advises that anyone who naps should set an alarm, because waking from deep sleep produces a heavy feeling that can last for half an hour. Some employers have therefore begun to provide quiet rooms, although others worry that staff will take advantage. Haddad answers that a rested worker who spends twenty minutes asleep at lunchtime is likely to be more productive than a tired one who spends the same time looking at a screen.

Modern technology is often blamed for poor sleep. Professor Tom Garrick showed that bright screens in the hour before bed delay the release of melatonin, a hormone that signals to the body that it is time to sleep. However, he points out that many people stay awake because of what they are doing on a device, such as reading stressful messages, and not because of the light. In his view, advice to buy special glasses or filters has been oversold; a better strategy is to put the phone away.

Taken together, these findings suggest some simple advice. Adults need between seven and nine hours; going to bed and rising at the same time each day helps; and the bedroom should be dark, quiet and cool. It would be foolish to treat sleep as a luxury to be traded for extra work, since people who do so tend, in the long run, to achieve less, not more. A tired employee makes more mistakes, forgets instructions and finds it harder to deal calmly with colleagues, so the hours saved are quickly lost again in repairing errors.
